topic: What if you acted like GTA 6 in real life for 24 hours?

script.text: One p.m. You and Mo jump into the back of a taxi. 'Follow that car!' you shout.
The driver looks at you in the mirror. 'Which car?' You point at a random blue one. He shrugs and follows it. For twenty minutes. Straight to a grocery store.
'That,' he says, 'was the most boring car chase of my life.' The meter says thirty-eight dollars. In the game, you'd just jump out and run.
So you do. And this is where real life stops being a game.
Running off without paying a taxi fare is a crime in most places. It's called theft of services. It's in the same family as shoplifting.

And that car outside the bakery this morning? Police take that very seriously, because that's how a lot of car thefts start. In the US, a car gets stolen about every thirty-two seconds. That's around a million cars a year. That's real.
The driver doesn't chase you. He doesn't need to. He has a dash camera, your face, and the exact spot where you got in.
Two p.m. Mo's video has fifty thousand views. Somebody recognized your hoodie. The one still hanging on the neighbor's fence.
Three p.m. You run a red light on the scooter. A camera flashes. In California, a red light ticket can cost close to five hundred dollars, once all the fees are added.
Four p.m. You add it up. The fence. The backyard. The scooter. The taxi. The car. In the game, each of those is nothing. Real life keeps a list. And real life doesn't reset when you reload.
Every one of those things has a name. Trespassing. Theft of services. A traffic violation. And thanks to Mo's video, every single one of them has evidence. In high definition.
Then you hear it. A siren. Getting closer.

science.claim: Leaving without paying a taxi fare is a crime in most places (theft of services / fare evasion).
science.working: Most US states have a 'theft of services' statute that covers obtaining transportation without paying, e.g. New York Penal Law 165.15; in England and Wales it is 'making off without payment' (Theft Act 1978, s.3).
science.source: New York Penal Law § 165.15; Theft Act 1978 s.3

science.claim: In the US a vehicle is stolen about every 32 seconds, around a million a year.
science.working: 1,020,729 vehicles were reported stolen in 2023; 365 x 24 x 3,600 / 1,020,729 = about 31 seconds.
science.source: National Insurance Crime Bureau, Vehicle Thefts Surge Nationwide in 2023 (April 2024)

science.claim: A red-light ticket in California can cost close to $500 with fees.
science.working: The base fine is $100, but penalty assessments and fees bring the total to about $490.
science.source: California Courts / California Vehicle Code 21453; widely cited total of about $490
